# Why metrics matter 📊 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Think about this 🤔
### A deceptively simple question

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 26px;"}

**Scenario**: You're building a model to predict whether patients have a rare disease that affects [1 in 1,000 people]{.alert}.

Your colleague shows you a model: ["It achieves 99.9% accuracy!"]{.alert}

:::{.fragment}
**Question**: Is this model any good?

Take 30 seconds to think about it...
:::

:::{.fragment}
**Hint**: What happens if the model simply [predicts "no disease" for every patient]{.alert}?
:::

:::{.fragment}
**The uncomfortable truth**: That "99.9% accurate" model [catches zero actual cases]{.alert}. Every sick patient is missed!
:::
:::

## The accuracy paradox
### When 99% accuracy is terrible

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- This is the [accuracy paradox]{.alert}
- Accuracy measures overall correctness, but doesn't tell us:
  - How many sick patients we found
  - How many false alarms we raised
  - Whether errors are concentrated in one group
- The problem is severe with [class imbalance]{.alert}
- Real examples:
  - Fraud: [0.2% of transactions]{.alert}
  - Security threats: [< 0.01%]{.alert} of events
  - Manufacturing defects: Often [< 1%]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![The accuracy paradox](figures/accuracy-paradox.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/accuracy-paradox.png"}

Source: [Medium](https://medium.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Classification metrics 🎯 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## The confusion matrix
### The foundation of classification evaluation

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- A table showing [all possible prediction outcomes]{.alert}
- Four key quantities:
  - **True Positives (TP)**: Correctly predicted positive
  - **True Negatives (TN)**: Correctly predicted negative
  - **False Positives (FP)**: Predicted +, actually − (Type I)
  - **False Negatives (FN)**: Predicted −, actually + (Type II)
- [All classification metrics derive from these four numbers!]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
| | Predicted + | Predicted − |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Actual +** | TP ✅ | FN ❌ |
| **Actual −** | FP ❌ | TN ✅ |

[![Confusion matrix](figures/confusion-matrix.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/confusion-matrix.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Precision and recall
### Two sides of the same coin

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Precision** = TP / (TP + FP)

- [When the model says "yes", how often is it right?]{.alert}
- High precision = few false alarms
- Important when [false positives are costly]{.alert}
- Examples: Spam detection, fraud alerts, product recommendations

**Recall** = TP / (TP + FN)

- [Of all actual positives, how many did we find?]{.alert}
- High recall = we don't miss positives
- Important when [false negatives are costly]{.alert}
- Examples: Cancer screening, security threats, safety systems
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Precision and recall](figures/precision.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/precision.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precision_and_recall)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The precision-recall trade-off
### You can't have it all

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Most classifiers output a [probability score]{.alert}
- We choose a [threshold]{.alert} to decide "positive" vs "negative"
- Moving the threshold trades off precision and recall:
  - **High threshold** (strict): High precision, low recall
  - **Low threshold** (lenient): High recall, low precision
- The [optimal threshold depends on your application!]{.alert}

**Quick question—which metric?**

| Scenario | Prioritise |
|----------|------------|
| Spam filter | [Precision]{.alert} |
| Cancer screening | [Recall]{.alert} |
| Airport security | [Recall]{.alert} |
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Precision-recall trade-off](figures/precision-recall-tradeoff.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/precision-recall-tradeoff.png"}

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## F1 score, ROC curves, and AUC
### Balancing and comparing

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
**F1 Score** = Harmonic mean of precision & recall

- Balances both in a single number
- F1 = 1 perfect, F1 = 0 worst
- Penalises extreme imbalances
- Popular for [imbalanced classification]{.alert}

| Precision | Recall | F1 Score |
|-----------|--------|----------|
| 0.80 | 0.80 | **0.80** |
| 0.80 | 0.20 | **0.32** |
| 1.00 | 0.01 | **0.02** |
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
**ROC Curve & AUC**

- Plots TPR vs FPR at all thresholds
- [AUC]{.alert} = Area Under Curve
- AUC = 0.5 → Random guessing
- AUC = 1.0 → Perfect classifier

[![ROC curve](figures/roc-curve.png){width="80%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/roc-curve.png"}
:::
:::
:::

## Regression metrics
### When the target is continuous

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
For regression (predicting numbers), we need different metrics:

| Metric | Intuition |
|--------|-----------|
| **MAE** | Average error size (in original units) |
| **MSE** | Average squared error (penalises big errors more) |
| **RMSE** | √MSE—same as MSE, but in original units |
| **R²** | Proportion of variance explained (0 to 1) |

:::{.fragment}
**Key intuitions:**

- **MAE**: "On average, predictions are off by X units"
- **RMSE**: "Typical error size, but big errors count more"
- **R²**: "The model explains X% of the variation" (R² = 0.8 means 80%)
:::
:::

# Validation & overfitting ⚠️ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## What is overfitting?
### The enemy of generalisation

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Overfitting]{.alert}: Model performs well on training data but poorly on new data
- The model has [memorised]{.alert} the training set, including its noise
- Signs of overfitting:
  - [Excellent training performance]{.alert}
  - [Poor test performance]{.alert}
  - Gap grows with model complexity
- Think of it like [memorising exam answers]{.alert} vs understanding the material
- The student who memorises fails when questions are rephrased
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Overfitting visualised](figures/overfitting.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/overfitting.png"}

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Underfitting vs overfitting
### Finding the sweet spot

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Underfitting, good fit, and overfitting](figures/overfit-underfit.png){width="70%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/overfit-underfit.png"}
:::

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=33%}
**Underfitting** 📉

- Model [too simple]{.alert}
- Poor on training AND test
- Can't capture the pattern
:::

:::{.column width=33%}
**Good fit** ✅

- [Right complexity]{.alert}
- Good on both sets
- Captures true pattern
:::

:::{.column width=33%}
**Overfitting** 📈

- Model [too complex]{.alert}
- Great on training, poor on test
- Memorised noise
:::
:::
:::

## Train, validation, and test splits
### The three-way split

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Training set** (~60-70%): Fit the model
- **Validation set** (~15-20%): Tune hyperparameters
- **Test set** (~15-20%): [Final evaluation (touch once!)]{.alert}
- [Never look at test data during model development!]{.alert}
- If you tune on test data, you're [cheating]{.alert}
- The test set must remain [truly unseen]{.alert}
- Think of test set as the [final exam]{.alert}—you shouldn't see questions while studying
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Train/validation/test split](figures/train-val-test.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/train-val-test.png"}

Source: [Machine Learning Mastery](https://machinelearningmastery.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Cross-validation
### Making the most of limited data

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- With small datasets, a single split may be [unreliable]{.alert}
- **K-fold cross-validation**:
  1. Split data into K equal folds
  2. Train on K-1 folds, validate on remaining fold
  3. Repeat K times, rotating validation fold
  4. Average the K results
- Common choices: K = 5 or K = 10
- Every data point used for both training and validation
- More [robust estimate]{.alert} of model performance
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![5-fold cross-validation](figures/cross-validation.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/cross-validation.png"}

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Preventing overfitting
### Your toolkit

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
| Technique | How it works |
|-----------|--------------|
| **More data** | Harder to memorise larger datasets |
| **Simpler model** | Reduce number of parameters |
| **Regularisation** | Penalise complex models (L1, L2) |
| **Early stopping** | Stop training before overfitting |
| **Dropout** | Randomly disable neurons in training |
| **Cross-validation** | Detect overfitting early |

> "All models are wrong, but some are useful." — George Box
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Training and validation curves](figures/learning-curves.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/learning-curves.png"}

The gap between curves indicates overfitting

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Evaluating text & language 📝 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## From classification to language generation
### New challenges emerge

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Classification: [One correct label per input]{.alert}
  - Cat or dog? → "Cat" or "Dog"
- Language generation: [Many valid outputs]{.alert}
  - "The cat sat on the mat" ≈ "A feline rested upon the rug"
- Traditional metrics struggle with this [one-to-many]{.alert} problem
- We need to measure:
  - [Fluency]{.alert}: Is the text grammatical?
  - [Relevance]{.alert}: Does it address the question?
  - [Factuality]{.alert}: Is it actually true?
- This is one of the [hardest problems]{.alert} in AI evaluation
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Language evaluation is challenging](figures/metrics-tradeoffs.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/metrics-tradeoffs.png"}

Source: [Analytics Vidhya](https://www.analyticsvidhya.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Perplexity
### How surprised is the model?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Perplexity]{.alert} measures how well a language model predicts text
- Intuition: [How many equally likely words could come next?]{.alert}
  - Perplexity of 10 → As uncertain as choosing from 10 random words
  - Perplexity of 100 → Much more uncertain
- Lower perplexity = model is [more confident]{.alert}
- Used to compare language models and track training progress

**The big limitation:**

Language models optimise for [fluency, not truthfulness]{.alert}. A confident lie still has low perplexity!
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
**Example:**

"The capital of France is ___"

- "Paris" → Low perplexity ✅
- "elephant" → High perplexity ❌

<br>

**But consider:**

"The earth is ___"

- "flat" → Could have [low perplexity]{.alert}!

<br>

[Fluency ≠ Factuality]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## BLEU and ROUGE
### Measuring text overlap

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=50%}
**BLEU** (for machine translation)

- Counts [n-gram matches]{.alert} between output and reference
- Focuses on [precision]{.alert}: What fraction of generated words match?
- Includes brevity penalty for short outputs
- Score from 0 to 1 (or 0 to 100)

**ROUGE** (for summarisation)

- Focuses on [recall]{.alert}: What fraction of reference words appear?
- ROUGE-1 (unigrams), ROUGE-2 (bigrams), ROUGE-L (longest common subsequence)
:::

:::{.column width=50%}
**Key limitations:**

- Don't understand [meaning]{.alert}
- Penalise valid [paraphrases]{.alert}
- Can't detect [factual errors]{.alert}
- Favour copying over abstraction

**Example:**

Reference: "The cat sat on the mat"

Output: "A feline rested on a rug"
→ Low BLEU (few matching words) despite [same meaning]{.alert}!

Output: "The mat sat on the cat"
→ Higher BLEU despite [wrong meaning]{.alert}!
:::
:::
:::

# Hallucinations 🎭 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## What are hallucinations?
### When AI confidently makes things up

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Hallucination]{.alert}: Fluent but factually incorrect or fabricated output
- The model generates plausible content [not grounded in reality]{.alert}
- Common forms:
  - **Fabricated citations**: Papers that don't exist
  - **Made-up statistics**: "73% of scientists agree..."
  - **False biographical details**: Wrong dates, achievements
  - **Confident nonsense**: Eloquent wrong explanations
- Why? Models predict [likely text]{.alert}, not [true text]{.alert}
- [This is one of the biggest challenges]{.alert} in deploying AI
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
**The core problem:**

Models optimise for:

`P(next word | context)`

Not for:

`P(statement is true)`

<br>

[![Hallucinations in AI](figures/data-leakage.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/data-leakage.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Real-world consequences
### Why hallucinations matter

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Notable incidents (all real!):**

- ⚖️ **Legal** (2023): Two lawyers cited [six non-existent cases]{.alert} from ChatGPT. They were sanctioned by the court.
- 🏥 **Medical**: AI chatbots gave [dangerous health advice]{.alert} citing fabricated studies
- 📰 **News**: AI-generated fake news [moved stock prices]{.alert}
- 📚 **Academic**: Students submitted essays with [invented references]{.alert}

**The stakes are rising:**

- More people trusting AI without verification
- Harder for non-experts to spot fabrications
- Legal and reputational risks for organisations
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}

**Discussion question:**

How would you verify if an AI's answer is correct?

- Check primary sources?
- Ask another AI?
- Trust your intuition?

[Critical thinking remains essential]{.alert}

<br>

🎬 [IBM: What Are AI Hallucinations?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cfqtFvWOfg0) (5 min)

<br>

[We'll explore hallucinations in depth in a later lecture!]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Detecting hallucinations
### Approaches and tools

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Detection methods:**

- **Manual verification**: Human fact-checkers (gold standard)
- **LLM-as-a-Judge**: Use one model to evaluate another
- **Consistency checks**: Ask the same question multiple ways
- **Cross-referencing**: Check against knowledge bases
- **Retrieval-based verification**: Look up claims in trusted sources

**Emerging metrics:**

- Faithfulness scores
- Groundedness measures
- Context adherence
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
**Mitigation strategies:**

- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)]{.alert}
  1. User asks question
  2. System retrieves relevant documents
  3. Model answers based on retrieved context
  4. Answer includes citations

- Chain-of-thought with citations
- Fine-tuning on verified data
- Teaching models to say "I don't know"

[We'll cover RAG in a future lecture!]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::

# Benchmarks & leaderboards 🏆 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## What are AI benchmarks?
### Standardised tests for AI systems

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Benchmarks]{.alert}: Standardised datasets and tasks to compare models
- Like academic exams, but for AI systems
- Famous examples:
  - **MMLU**: 57 subjects of academic knowledge
  - **HellaSwag**: Commonsense reasoning
  - **TruthfulQA**: Resistance to misconceptions
  - **HumanEval**: Code generation
- Enable [objective comparison]{.alert} across different models
- Drive progress by setting clear targets
- Track capability improvements over time
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![AI benchmarks](figures/class-imbalance.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/class-imbalance.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The leaderboard culture
### Benefits and risks

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Public leaderboards rank models by benchmark scores
- [Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard]{.alert} is hugely influential
- **Benefits:**
  - Encourages [transparency]{.alert}
  - Enables [fair comparison]{.alert}
  - Tracks [progress]{.alert} over time
  - Creates healthy [competition]{.alert}
- **Risks:**
  - Overfitting to benchmarks
  - Gaming through contamination
  - Neglecting unmeasured capabilities

**Try it:** [huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceH4/open_llm_leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceH4/open_llm_leaderboard)
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Hugging Face Leaderboard](figures/slice-performance.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/slice-performance.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The dark side of benchmarks
### When metrics become targets

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
[Goodhart's Law]{.alert}: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"

**Common problems:**

- **Benchmark contamination**: Test data in training data—memorisation not generalisation
- **Teaching to the test**: Optimise for quirks, not capability
- **Metric saturation**: "Human-level" on benchmarks but fails in practice
- **Narrow focus**: Only measuring what's easy to measure

**What benchmarks miss:**

- Real-world robustness
- Safety and alignment
- Creative problem-solving
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Goodhart's Law](figures/goodharts-law.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/goodharts-law.png"}

Source: [Thomas & Uminsky (2022)](https://www.cell.com/patterns/fulltext/S2666-3899(22)00056-3)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Ethics beyond accuracy 🤔 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Fairness: When overall accuracy hides problems
### The disaggregation imperative

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Overall accuracy can hide [serious failures for specific groups]{.alert}
- **Real example** (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018):
  - Commercial face recognition error rates:
  - Light-skinned men: [0.8% error]{.alert}
  - Dark-skinned women: [34.7% error]{.alert}
  - 43× worse performance for one group!
- This is called [data slicing]{.alert} or [subgroup analysis]{.alert}
- Even removing sensitive features doesn't help—they correlate with other features
- [Always evaluate models per subgroup]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Subgroup performance disparities](figures/slice-performance.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/slice-performance.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2024/data-centric-evaluation/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Fairness metrics
### Quantifying equity

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Key fairness metrics:**

- **Demographic parity**: Equal positive prediction rates across groups
- **Equalised odds**: Equal TPR and FPR across groups
- **Predictive parity**: Equal precision across groups

**The impossibility theorem:**

[Cannot satisfy all fairness criteria simultaneously]{.alert} (except in special cases)

- Mathematical fact, not a failure of effort
- Different metrics encode different [values]{.alert}
- Choice of fairness metric is a [value judgment]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Fairness in ML](figures/fairness-metrics.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/fairness-metrics.png"}

Source: [Google AI](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/fairness-overview)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Distribution shift
### When the world changes

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Models trained on [historical data]{.alert}
- Real world [changes over time]{.alert}
- [Distribution shift]{.alert}: Mismatch between training and deployment

**Three types:**

1. **Covariate shift**: Inputs change (trained SF, deployed Boston)
2. **Concept shift**: Relationships change (fraud patterns evolve)
3. **Label shift**: Class frequencies change (COVID positivity rates)

**Solutions:**

- Monitor performance continuously
- Retrain when metrics degrade
- Use robust validation strategies
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2023/imbalance-outliers-shift/)
:::

# Practical considerations 🛠️ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Choosing the right metrics
### A decision framework

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}

| Question | If yes... |
|----------|-----------|
| Is false positive cost high? | Prioritise [precision]{.alert} |
| Is false negative cost high? | Prioritise [recall]{.alert} |
| Are classes imbalanced? | Use [F1 or AUC]{.alert}, not accuracy |
| Is it a generation task? | Need [text-specific metrics]{.alert} + human eval |
| Are multiple groups affected? | Check [fairness metrics]{.alert} per group |
| Will data change over time? | Plan for [distribution shift]{.alert} monitoring |

:::{.fragment}
**Golden rule:** [No single metric is sufficient]{.alert}. Use a dashboard of complementary measures.
:::
:::

## Building your evaluation strategy
### Putting it all together

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**A practical framework:**

1. **Define success** — What does "good enough" mean?
2. **Choose primary metrics** — Based on error costs
3. **Add secondary metrics** — Fairness, latency, cost
4. **Set up monitoring** — Track over time
5. **Plan for failure** — What when metrics degrade?
6. **Document choices** — Why these metrics?

**Remember:**

- Start simple, iterate
- Involve stakeholders
- Metrics shape incentives—choose wisely
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
**Example dashboard:**

| Metric | Value | Status |
|--------|-------|--------|
| F1 (overall) | 0.87 | ✅ |
| F1 (group A) | 0.89 | ✅ |
| F1 (group B) | 0.71 | ⚠️ |
| Latency (p95) | 120ms | ✅ |
| Fairness gap | 18% | ⚠️ |

[Evaluation is ongoing, not one-time]{.alert}

[Monitor, don't just measure]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::

# Summary ✅ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Main takeaways

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}

- `r fa('exclamation-triangle')` [Accuracy alone is dangerous]{.alert}—especially for imbalanced classes

- `r fa('balance-scale')` [Precision vs recall]{.alert} trade-off depends on cost of errors

- `r fa('chart-line')` [Validation is essential]{.alert}—never evaluate on training data

- `r fa('language')` [Text evaluation is hard]{.alert}—BLEU/ROUGE measure overlap, not meaning

- `r fa('ghost')` [Hallucinations]{.alert} are a fundamental challenge—more in a later lecture

- `r fa('trophy')` [Benchmarks help but mislead]{.alert}—beware Goodhart's Law

- `r fa('users')` [Fairness requires]{.alert} looking beyond aggregate metrics
:::
